courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Why radiance fields needed a rasterizer instead of ray marching
md: 3DGS keeps NeRF's blending formula but replaces the implicit neural field with explicit primitives. Explicit primitives can be projected and rasterized, so rendering cost scales with the number of splats that touch a pixel, not with hundreds of network queries per ray.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: LL/SC: watching the location instead of its value
md: Portable C and C++ code does not get LL/SC semantics. `compare_exchange` is defined as a value comparison; on an LL/SC machine the compiler builds it from an LL/SC loop that starts *after* your earlier plain load of `top`. The window where ABA strikes (between that load and the CAS) is outside the reservation, so ABA is back.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Interaction effects and Shapley values
md: Shapley values are a summary, not a full account. They need $v$ for all $2^n$ configurations (16 here; for many components, sampled orders are the usual approximation). They hide that P is harmful without R, and they average over queries. Report the interaction cells and per-query spread too.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Missing function-level checks and privilege escalation
md: Every function has an owner question (which roles may call it) and every object has one (which users may touch it). A request must pass both. Hiding buttons and URLs answers neither.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: What Active Directory is: one directory for thousands of machines
md: AD is a replicated database of identities and rules. DCs hold it, LDAP reads it, Kerberos and NTLM use it to sign people in, and GPOs push its settings to machines. Every attack in this course either steals proof of an identity or gains the right to write to this database.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Delegation: letting a server act as you, and how it goes wrong
md: Delegation lets a service obtain tickets as its users. Unconstrained trusts the server with users' TGTs; constrained trusts it with a list of back ends; RBCD lets the back end decide. Keep admins non-delegable, remove unconstrained delegation, and watch 4742 and 5136 for delegation changes.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Tiered administration, Protected Users and LAPS
md: Keep powerful credentials off weak machines: tier admin accounts, use PAWs, put admins in Protected Users, mark them non-delegable, rotate local admin passwords with LAPS and service passwords with gMSAs.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: JScript, VBScript and HTA: script hosts and their process trees
md: Node's documentation is blunt: 'The node:vm module is not a security mechanism. Do not use it to run untrusted code.' The fakes give visibility, not safety. Run emulation only inside the isolated analysis VM, exactly as you would run the sample itself.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: The exploit lifecycle: bug, primitive, leak, control, payload
md: Exploitation is a ladder of capabilities: bug, primitive, leak, control, payload. Every mitigation removes or weakens one rung, and the earlier the rung, the more bug-specific and costly the attacker's workaround.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Red team, pentest, purple team: three different questions
md: Pentest: find and fix weaknesses in a scope. Red team: measure whether people, process and technology detect and respond to a realistic adversary. Purple team: improve detection together, technique by technique. Adversary emulation is the method underneath the last two: play a specific, intelligence-backed threat.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Case: CISA's red team at a critical infrastructure organisation
md: A red team report is most valuable when it records, for every step, what the defenders should have seen and did not. AA23-059A does this in both phases, which is why its findings turn directly into detections and hardening work.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: tau-bench: simulated users, database state and pass^k
md: pass@k rewards finding a solution in k tries (useful when a verifier can pick the winner). pass^k rewards solving it every time (what a deployed agent needs). For independent trials with success p they are $1-(1-p)^k$ and $p^k$; across tasks, pass^k depends heavily on how p is spread.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Why an agent cannot just replay its whole history
md: Misconception: a memory layer makes the agent remember *better* than full history. On LoCoMo, where a conversation still fits in the window, full context scored highest in the Mem0 paper. Memory wins when history no longer fits, or when the cost and latency of re-reading it every turn are unacceptable.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Layer the checks: deterministic first, judges last
md: The multiplication assumes independent errors, which is optimistic. A judge and a test suite written from the same misunderstanding of the spec fail on the same wrong answers, so the real chain FPR is higher than the product.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: The map: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025
md: LLM09 Misinformation is closer to reliability than to classic security, and other frameworks would not list it. It still lands companies in court (lesson 15), so engineers own it too.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Improper output handling: model output is untrusted input
md: "The model wrote it, so it's ours" is the mistake. Output is shaped by every token in the context, including retrieved pages and emails. Validate it exactly as strictly as you would a form field from an anonymous user.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Testing it: red teaming, benchmarks and AI for defenders
md: Measure both utility and attack success, test with adaptive and varied attacks, and prefer defences whose success does not depend on recognising the attack's wording.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: The soft watermark: add delta to the green logits
md: $\delta$ trades watermark strength against quality; $\gamma$ sets how often human text hits green by chance. The detector depends only on $\gamma$ and the hash rule, never on $\delta$, so a provider can change $\delta$ per product without changing the detector.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Watermarking images, audio and video
md: Post-hoc pixel marks are cheap and model-agnostic but live in a thin perturbation that regeneration can wash out. In-model marks are tied to one generator: Stable Signature to its decoder, which a different VAE bypasses; Tree-Ring to the starting noise, which resists mild regeneration better but needs the model to detect. Every image scheme sets its threshold with the same binomial or Gaussian null as text.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Isolation Forest: anomalies split off in fewer random cuts
md: The fixed 0.5 cutoff of contamination="auto" is not calibrated to your data. In the 1000-point evaluation set of lesson 5 it flags 241 points when only 10 are anomalies. Rank by score, or set the threshold from a review budget, rather than trusting the default label.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: APIs from zero: REST, GraphQL and what a request carries
md: Misconception: "Only our app calls this API, so it is private." The app's traffic can be read and replayed by anyone who installs it, and API keys built into an app can be extracted from it. Treat every request as if a stranger typed it by hand.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Redirect URIs, the state parameter and OAuth CSRF
md: Misconception: state is optional decoration. Without state, PKCE, or nonce, any OAuth client can be logged into an attacker's account. RFC 6749 and RFC 9700 both make CSRF protection a must.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Case: Storm-0558 and the forged Microsoft tokens (2023)
md: A valid signature is only as good as the question "is this key one that this issuer uses for this kind of token?" RFC 8725 says it plainly: check that the keys belong to the issuer. And signing keys are crown jewels: rotate them, retire them, alert on their age, and log every use.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Secure code review: what a reviewer looks for
md: Review the flows, not the lines. For every value from outside, follow it to each sink and check the control at each trust boundary. Then ask the questions a tool cannot: should this exist, and who may use it?

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: CVE assignment and CNAs: who names a vulnerability
md: Fewer CVEs is not the same as fewer vulnerabilities. A vendor that fixes bugs silently looks clean while customers' scanners have nothing to match and never flag the old version. Judge vendors by how fast and how well they publish, not by the count.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: LSNs, pageLSN and the two tables recovery rebuilds
md: Do not mix up pageLSN and recLSN. In the example, P1 was first dirtied at LSN 10 and last changed at 60, so its recLSN is 10 while its pageLSN is 60. recLSN says where redo for the page might need to start; pageLSN says which changes the page already contains.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: A toy run: how the input type flips the top result
md: Simplified: real embeddings are not interpretable feature lists, and the size of the effect varies by model and corpus. The toy shows the direction of the failure, not its typical magnitude. Lesson 5 is about measuring the magnitude on your data.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Why waiting on threads is expensive and coroutines are cheap
md: Async does not make one request faster. It makes **waiting cheap**: a waiting connection costs a small saved object instead of a blocked OS thread with its own stack, so a few threads can serve many thousands of mostly idle connections.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Compare-and-swap: write only if nothing changed, else retry
md: CAS compares values, not history. If the value goes from A to B and back to A between your load and your CAS, the CAS succeeds as if nothing happened. For a counter that is harmless. For pointers in lock-free data structures (structures built from atomics instead of locks) it can be a real bug, the **ABA problem**, which has its own course later.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Who are you, prove it, and what may you do?
md: Identification is a claim, authentication is proof of the claim, authorization is permission. MFA means two different *kinds* of factor, not two secrets of the same kind.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: After login: session tokens, fixation, expiry and logout
md: A session token is a password with an expiry date. Make it random (64+ bits), send it only as a Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookie, replace it at login, expire it on the server, and destroy it on the server at logout.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Orchestrator, parallel subagents and context isolation
md: More subagents is not automatically better. Anthropic's early agents spawned 50 subagents for simple queries and distracted each other with updates. Their prompts now embed effort rules: simple fact-finding gets 1 agent with 3 to 10 tool calls, direct comparisons get 2 to 4 subagents with 10 to 15 calls each, and complex research uses more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: On-demand capacity: tokens per minute and the max_tokens trap
md: Specific burndown rates, default quotas and tier prices change as models launch. Treat any number you remember as stale and read the current quota page and model card before you size a workload.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Firmware images: layout, signatures and entropy
md: Firmware analysis starts with layout, not code: find the magic numbers, check the headers' sizes and CRCs, map the entropy, carve each region, and repeat on what comes out. Only then pick the CPU and load address for the disassembler.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Why a pipelined CPU has to guess at every branch
md: A correctly predicted branch is nearly free. A mispredicted one costs about as many cycles as the pipeline is deep. Agner Fog, whose optimization manuals measure these costs on real chips, gives roughly 0 to 2 cycles for a predicted branch and about 15 to 25 cycles for a misprediction on modern x86 cores.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: The LSM write path: memtable, flush and immutable SSTables
md: LSM reads search from newest to oldest and stop at the first entry for the key, whether that is a value or a tombstone. Correctness depends only on this ordering, never on old versions being gone.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: LRU, CLOCK and PostgreSQL clock-sweep on a 4-frame pool
md: CLOCK is not "LRU but cheaper" in every case. It only approximates recency, and when all bits are set it evicts in plain circular order. Its win is that a hit costs one bit or counter update with no shared list to reorder.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: MTD, RTO and RPO: the arithmetic and the dependency trap
md: RTO plus reprocessing time must fit inside the MTD. A service's achievable RTO is the longest path through its dependencies, so shared components inherit the shortest targets. State RPO per failure type: replication protects against losing a site, not against bad writes.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Designing the backup set: 3-2-1-1-0, schedules and retention
md: Choose the backup type by restore chain, the frequency by RPO, the retention by how late you will notice damage (by time, never by count), and the locations by failure domain, including the provider's own control plane. 3-2-1-1-0 adds an immutable copy and zero errors on verified restores.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Exercising the plan: tabletops, functional tests, failovers and chaos
md: Exercises fail when they are rigged to pass: announced weeks ahead, run by the people who wrote the plan, on a quiet Sunday, with the expert in the room. Inject realistic constraints (a key person unavailable, the wiki down, a backup from yesterday rather than an hour ago) and record measured times, not opinions.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Inside BLT: local encoder, latent Transformer, local decoder
md: Encoder: bytes plus hashed n-grams, pooled into patch vectors by masked cross-attention. Latent Transformer: the expensive part, once per patch. Decoder: bytes query the output of the patch before theirs to predict the next byte.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: The same bugs in Rust: compile errors, panics, and what slips through
md: Misconception: "Rust has no runtime checks, everything is proven at compile time." Lifetimes and aliasing are checked at compile time; indexing, `RefCell` borrows and debug-mode overflow are checked at run time. The design goal is that every remaining failure is defined, not that there are none.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: FFI: calling C from Rust without losing track of ownership
md: Undefined behavior does not stay on its side of the boundary. The Rust Reference notes that UB in a called C function makes the whole program undefined, including the Rust parts, and vice versa. FFI bindings are one of the most common reasons real code needs unsafe, so keep them thin and wrap them in a safe API.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Writes, sharing between cores, and measuring your machine
md: Do not hard-code 64 just because it is common. Query the line size: Drepper suggests asking getconf for it at build time and handing it to the compiler as a macro definition (`-DCLS=$(getconf LEVEL1_DCACHE_LINESIZE)`), and if a binary must run everywhere, use the largest line size it may meet.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: What attribution graphs found: arithmetic, languages, refusals, CoT
md: Confirmed by intervention: the addition lookup swap (1995 to 1998), the three multilingual edits, known-answer features gating hallucination, ablations that change refusals, and the hint-driven backward reasoning. Graph readings only: no carrying in the model's arithmetic, English as default, and anything involving attention, such as why the model attends to the hint or why "However" needs a new sentence.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Small propensities, high variance, and clipping
md: Clipping changes what the estimator measures. A clipped rank is systematically undervalued, which pushes documents shown low back down, the same direction as the original position bias. Tune $\tau$ on held-out data and report it.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Second lines of defence: strict CSP and Trusted Types
md: Trusted Types changes the review question from "is any of our thousands of DOM writes unsafe?" to "are our two or three policies correct?". The browser enforces that nothing else reaches a sink.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Image search with CLIP, the modality gap, and where it fails
md: Do not compare scores across modalities with one threshold. Image-image cosines and text-image cosines come from different regions of the space, so a cutoff tuned for text queries will not transfer to image queries, and a mixed index of image and text vectors will tend to rank same-modality items together.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Compromised instance forensics: protect, snapshot, memory, isolate
md: Misconception: "applying the quarantine security group cuts the attacker off". It stops new connections. Existing tracked connections continue until they time out, so verify with flow logs or host telemetry that the session actually ended, and use a network ACL or a stop when it has not.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Service control policies in depth: inheritance and exemptions
md: SCPs combine by intersection down the tree: an Allow is needed at every level, and a Deny at any level wins. Prefer deny-list SCPs on top of FullAWSAccess, exempt only named platform or break-glass roles through `aws:PrincipalArn`, and test every change in a staging OU first.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: CSPM, CIEM and CNAPP, and a full architecture review
md: A good cloud architecture assumes one credential, one function or one account will fail, and makes sure that failure stays small: walls between accounts, guardrails nobody can lift, no hidden paths to admin, no standing human keys, logs and backups out of reach. Posture tools help you keep it that way; they do not design it for you.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Storage exposure: public buckets, Block Public Access and SAS tokens
md: Turn on the provider's public-access guardrail at the highest level you can (organization or account), and treat any exception as a reviewed, documented decision. Then scan for anything public anyway: IAM Access Analyzer in AWS reports buckets shared publicly or with other accounts.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Gaussian mixtures and EM: soft k-means with a shape per cluster
md: k-means is EM for a Gaussian mixture with one shared, fixed, vanishing round covariance. Free the covariances and you gain soft memberships and per-cluster shapes; you also gain more parameters to estimate, and a new way to fail.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Why analytic scans want columns, not rows
md: Columns win when queries read few columns of many rows; rows win for point reads and frequent updates of whole records. The layout decides how many bytes a scan must move.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inside the optimizer: IR, SSA and the classic scalar passes
md: Misconception: "the optimizer understands what my code is for." It does not. Each pass applies one local rewrite it can prove safe, and the big wins come from chains: inlining exposes a constant, propagation folds it, DCE deletes the leftovers. When a chain breaks (a call it cannot see into, a pointer that might alias), every later step is lost.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: LTO and ThinLTO: optimizing across source files
md: Without LTO, a .c file is the optimizer's horizon. LTO stores the compiler's IR in the object files and optimizes the whole program at link time. ThinLTO does the global analysis on small summaries and the heavy work in parallel, so it scales and supports incremental builds.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Grounding: Set-of-Mark labels, DOM and accessibility trees
md: Misconception: Set-of-Mark always improves GUI grounding. Both SeeAct and OSWorld saw marks underperform richer text grounding on dense screens. Marks help most when there are few, well-separated elements.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: ThreadSanitizer: catching races with vector clocks at runtime
md: TSan reports races that **did not cause a failure** in this run. It needs only that both conflicting accesses execute and that nothing orders them by happens-before. That is its big advantage over stress testing.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Linearizability: one copy, respecting real time
md: A read that overlaps a write may return either the old or the new value. Once any read has returned the new value and completed, every later-starting read must return it too. Linearizability forbids the value from flickering back.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Consistent hashing with bounded loads: a hard cap per server
md: Bounded loads caps *load per server*, not *load per key*. If one key alone exceeds a server's capacity, forwarding spreads its requests across servers only when any server can answer for it, as with a cache that can fetch from the origin. A database shard that alone holds the data still needs the replication or splitting tools from the previous lesson.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Arc consistency: AC-3 prunes domains before guessing
md: Arc consistency is not the same as a solution. Three variables with domain $\{1,2\}$ and pairwise $\neq$ constraints are fully arc-consistent (every value has a support on every arc), yet no assignment satisfies all three. Propagation shrinks the search; it does not replace it.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: What ships in an image: base images, distroless and scanning
md: Ship the least software that runs your app: multi-stage builds into a minimal or distroless base, scanned in CI and rescanned while running.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: RBAC: roles, bindings and the permissions that escalate
md: RBAC only adds. Grant namespaced Roles with explicit resources, names and verbs. Treat Secrets list, pod creation, nodes/proxy, escalate, bind and impersonate as administrator-level rights.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Secrets: base64 is not encryption
md: base64 hides nothing. Lock down who can get, list or watch Secrets and who can create pods, encrypt etcd data with a KMS provider, rewrite existing Secrets after enabling it, and keep high-value credentials in an external store.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Why a multi-turn search needs explicit state
md: The state object, not the transcript, is the source of truth for what the user wants right now. The LLM proposes changes to it; code applies them; the query is a pure function of it.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: When to ask a clarifying question instead of guessing
md: Do not ask about what the state already answers, or about slots marked dontcare. Repeated or redundant questions are the fastest way to make mixed-initiative feel worse than a plain search box.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Do reasoning models admit the hints they use?
md: When the model can act on information without reasoning about it, its CoT usually stays silent about it, even with no pressure to hide. CoT monitoring then helps you notice frequent behaviors, but it cannot certify that a behavior is absent.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Why CoT is monitorable at all, and how to keep it so
md: A clean CoT is not evidence of safety for tasks that do not need a CoT. Chen et al. and Korbak et al. both warn that malign reasoning can happen in activations, so a monitoring-only safety case (an argument that a model is safe to deploy) fails there.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Inside the forward pass: query and document attend to each other
md: The cost problem of cross-encoders is not mainly the quadratic attention. It is that the full model, linear layers included, runs for every pair at query time. A bi-encoder pays the same per-token cost too, but for the documents only once, offline.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Block ciphers: what AES actually does to 16 bytes
md: A block cipher on its own encrypts exactly one block. Real messages are many blocks, and how you chain them (the **mode**) decides whether patterns leak. Calling raw AES block by block is the mistake of the next lesson.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Sound primitives, broken systems: how crypto use fails
md: Strong algorithms fail through their callers. When reviewing crypto, ask what the attacker can choose, what they can observe, what must never repeat, what is compared, and whether each key has one job. The rest of this course is those five questions applied to real failures.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Randomness in practice: weak, shared and first-boot keys
md: A random-looking key tells you nothing about how many keys were possible. Weak keys from Debian, Android and the Ps and Qs devices all looked perfectly random one at a time; the problem only shows when you compare many.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: CuTe layouts: shape and stride as an index function
md: A CuTe layout is not limited to row- or column-major, and the index it returns is in elements of whatever it is applied to, not bytes. The same function can index global memory, shared memory, registers, or even map thread ids to coordinates.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
md: Pooling does not make stranding vanish. In the toy pooled design, host D still has 64 GB of local DRAM it cannot sell. Pooling helps because the *peaks* of different hosts rarely line up, so a shared buffer can be smaller than the sum of per-host slack.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The CFAA: access, authorisation, damage and loss
md: Two failure modes for beginners: thinking "no damage, no crime" ((a)(2) only needs access plus obtaining information), and thinking "no money taken, no loss" (response costs are loss).

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Crossing borders: the Budapest Convention and jurisdiction
md: Budapest Convention (2001): common offences (Articles 2 to 6, with a carve-out for authorised testing), procedural powers, and cooperation: fast preservation (up to 90 days domestically; at least 60 days for a foreign request) and a 24/7 contact network.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Monitoring, interception and privacy law in security work
md: Before monitoring: who authorised it, were users informed, and is this the least intrusive data that answers the question? Prefer metadata to content, pseudonymise identifiers, limit retention, and never repurpose what you saw.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a researcher's decision checklist
md: Authority, jurisdiction, minimum data, other laws, harm to people, records and reporting. Run all six before you touch what is not yours, and keep the evidence that you did.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Mixtures that change during training: annealing data and mid-training
md: Modern mixtures are schedules. A long first stage uses a broad mix; a short final stage, run while the learning rate decays to zero, upweights the best small sources (repeated a few times if needed). The same short anneal doubles as a cheap test of whether a new dataset is worth adding.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Worked example: binary search over animation keyframes
md: Measure what the hot path *reads repeatedly*. Splitting the search key from its payload shrinks the working set the loop revisits, which often matters more than the miss count of a single call.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Encryption at rest, layer by layer: disk, database, field
md: "Encrypted at rest" in a compliance checklist usually means disk, storage or TDE encryption. It answers stolen hardware and copied backups. It does nothing against SQL access, application bugs or stolen credentials, which is how most data is actually taken.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Media sanitisation: clear, purge and destroy (NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2)
md: On SSDs and flash, never trust file shredders or multi-pass overwrites. Use the drive's sanitise command or cryptographic erase (and verify the result), or physically destroy it. In the cloud, crypto erase of keys you control is usually the only purge you can perform.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Making rare states common: faults, BUGGIFY and swarm testing
md: To find rare bugs, maximize the *diversity* of runs, not the intensity of each one. Random per-run choices of faults, features and buggify sites cover far more distinct states than one heavily tuned configuration.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Reviewing infrastructure as code: reading a Terraform plan
md: The most dangerous line in a plan is often not an open port but a `-/+` or `-` on something stateful: a database, a bucket, a KMS key. Replacements are triggered by innocent-looking edits (a renamed resource, a changed engine version), and a reviewer skimming for security groups will miss them.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Build it: turn your GPT into a masked diffusion LM
md: Three edits turn a GPT into a masked diffusion LM: a [MASK] id, `is_causal=False`, and targets at the same positions as the inputs. In practice add a fourth, relative positions such as RoPE, so the bidirectional model learns locality quickly. At equal size and steps it trains to a worse likelihood than the GPT, and its samples get better as each pass commits fewer tokens.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs
md: Goodput = the highest rate at which at least 90% (or your target) of requests meet every latency SLO, divided by the GPUs used. It is the number disaggregation is designed to raise.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Eight NTFS timestamps, and how timestomping gets caught
md: One timestamp is a claim. Two attributes, a journal, a log and telemetry that agree are a finding. Write the finding with the corroboration, not the single field.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Evidence law and writing the expert report
md: Artefacts identify accounts, devices and volumes, not people. The BTK disk said "Dennis" and a church; identity came from DNA. Write "the account dennis" or "a user of this profile", unless other evidence puts a person at the keyboard.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Build it: a DPO run from preference data to evaluation
md: A DPO run is four steps: pairs (often AI-judged, like UltraFeedback), masked summed log-probs for policy and reference, the loss plus logged implicit rewards, and a length-aware evaluation of generated answers. Test the plumbing with ln 2 at step 0 and a padding-invariance check.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: How dual writes silently diverge, and how to contain it
md: Two independent writes have no shared order and no shared atomicity. Either keep one store authoritative and repair the other, or derive the second store from the first store's commit log.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Why run your tracing logic inside the kernel
md: The verifier is a **safety** check, not a security review. It proves your program cannot crash or hang the kernel; it does not judge what the program observes. That is why loading tracing programs requires root, or both the CAP_BPF and CAP_PERFMON capabilities (slices of root's privilege granted on their own: CAP_BPF for loading BPF programs and maps, CAP_PERFMON for tracing).

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it
md: Order of operations for edge models: pick an efficient architecture and distill into it, quantize to int8 with per-channel weights, fall back to QAT if accuracy drops, prune only when your runtime benefits, and verify accuracy, latency and peak RAM on the actual device.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Exposure management: what you show the internet, continuously
md: Exposure management is attack surface discovery plus judgement plus follow-through: see what the internet sees, tie each item to an owner and to what attackers are exploiting, and verify every fix from the outside.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Measuring wasted tokens and training them away
md: Cutting after the first correct answer is the most aggressive compression, and it costs accuracy on hard problems. The useful target is 'one solve plus one check', not 'one solve'.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Budget forcing, effort levels and hard caps at inference
md: A small output-token cap is not a cheap way to get short reasoning. The model does not know about the cap, so it can be cut off mid-thought, and you pay for the thinking tokens with nothing to show. Use the effort or budget control that the model was trained to respond to.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Worked configs: SwiftOnSecurity's sysmon-config and sysmon-modular
md: A Sysmon config is a written decision about what you will be able to investigate later. Read what your config excludes as carefully as what it includes, and keep it in version control like detection rules (logging-detection-engineering).

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: One meter, many appliances: the disaggregation problem
md: Real aggregates are not the clean sum of the appliances you know about. UK-DALE reports that in House 1, with monitors on almost every appliance, only 80% of the energy was sub-metered, partly because the 52 plug monitors themselves draw about 50 W. The $\varepsilon_t$ term is never zero.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Cleaning: Unicode, case, punctuation and legal suffixes
md: Stripping is lossy. NFKC turns the superscript in `i⁹` into a plain `9`, and a stopword list (words deleted from every key because they seem uninformative) that drops `group`, `bank` or `the` can merge different companies. Strip only tokens that never distinguish entities in your data, apply cleaning to the matching key, and keep the original string.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: A tenant: the cloud directory behind every Microsoft 365 login
md: A tenant is a token issuer that many services trust. The questions that decide its security are: who can get a token, for which app, with which permissions, from where, and for how long.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Case: Midnight Blizzard inside Microsoft's own tenant (2024)
md: Midnight Blizzard turned one unprotected account into mailbox access through apps: find an app with power, create apps of your own, grant them an application permission. Defend by inventorying every tenant and app, enforcing MFA everywhere, and alerting on grants of high-risk application permissions.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Token theft and replay, and binding tokens to devices
md: Passkeys protect the login; device binding protects what the login produces. Use both, plus a compliant-device requirement, and keep revocation and CAE ready for the replay that gets through.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: The logs: sign-ins, audit, Graph activity and MailItemsAccessed
md: Sign-in logs say who got tokens, audit logs say what changed, Graph activity logs say what apps asked for, and MailItemsAccessed says which mail was touched. Export all four before you need them: default retention is 7 or 30 days.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: The winner's curse: why the best public score is too high
md: The maximum of many noisy scores is biased upward. Selecting a system on a query set uses up that set: its score for the winner is no longer an unbiased estimate. The bias grows with the number of systems tried (roughly like sqrt(ln N)) and shrinks with more queries (like 1/sqrt(n)).

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Contamination: when test queries leak into training data
md: Putting it together: split by query cluster and time, tune on dev, read a sealed and rotating test set rarely, report paired bootstrap CIs, correct for every comparison you run, and check for contamination with fresh queries the model could not have seen.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: What each mitigation does not stop, and where to practise
md: Combine layers so their blind spots do not line up: canary plus shadow stack or PAC for returns, CFI for forward edges, full RELRO for the GOT, PIE with high-entropy ASLR and no leaks, tagging or hardened allocators for the heap, and a sandbox around anything that parses untrusted input. Then keep fixing bugs.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds
md: A common misreading is that FedAvg averages the clients' answers. It averages their **parameters**. In this problem the sample-weighted average of the three local optima is 1.667 and the plain average is 2.0, while the true optimum is 2.3. Averaging models that have fully solved their own problems gives the wrong model.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-1: expand at search time instead of build time
md: ACORN-$\gamma$ and ACORN-1 run the same search strategy, predicate subgraph traversal. They differ only in *where* the denser neighborhood comes from: stored at build time (ACORN-$\gamma$, faster search, slower build) or reconstructed from two-hop lookups at query time (ACORN-1, cheap build, somewhat slower search).

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Online softmax: exact attention one block at a time
md: Online softmax is exact. The running max is only for numerical safety (keeping $e^x$ from overflowing); any consistent reference point gives the same $O/l$. Every FlashAttention version computes the same math; they differ only in how the work is mapped onto the hardware.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: The training target: straight lines and their velocity
md: The training loss does not go to zero even for a perfect network. Different pairs pass through the same $(x_t, t)$ with different targets, and a regression can only output their average. That average is the field you want, as lesson 3 shows.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Refinement: proving a detailed design implements an abstract one
md: Implementation is implication: the detailed spec, seen through a refinement mapping, must allow only behaviors the abstract spec allows. Extra internal steps are fine because they map to stuttering steps.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: What 8 and 4 bits can hold: E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1
md: Exponent bits buy **range**, mantissa bits buy **precision**. E4M3 rounds with at most 6.25% relative error but spans only about 18 binades; E5M2 spans about 32 binades at 12.5%; E2M1 (FP4) spans 3.58 binades at up to 25%.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: NVFP4: 16-value blocks, E4M3 scales and a tensor scale
md: In NVFP4 the amax of every 16-value block is encoded at close to FP8 precision (the block scale is E4M3), which is at least 1/16 = 6.25% of all values. MXFP4 stores every value, the amax included, at FP4 precision behind a power-of-two scale.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Network and device signals: IPs, proxies and fingerprints
md: Never trust a device signal you did not verify. A header or a JavaScript value is a claim made by the client. Use it to raise suspicion when claims disagree or repeat across many accounts, not to grant trust on its own.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Promotion and referral abuse: multi-accounting and holds
md: Every promotion is a price per account. Tie it to a scarce identity, check the link between referrer and referee, and hold the payout until the qualifying payment can no longer be reversed.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: From risk score to decision: rules, models, step-up and review
md: Pick actions by expected cost: allow when $pL$ is small, block when $(1-p)G$ is small, and step up in between when the challenge catches more fraud than it costs in lost customers.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
md: Calling fsync on a file does not necessarily make the file's **directory entry** durable. A newly created or renamed file also needs an fsync on a file descriptor for the directory, or after a crash the name may be missing.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: A real hunt with libFuzzer: harness, run log and the crash
md: A harness plus a sanitizer turns 'run the parser on generated bytes' into an automatic bug finder: coverage guidance reaches deep code, comparison tracing gets past magic values, and ASan converts silent corruption into a report with a saved reproducer.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Protocol and stateful fuzzing, and the Broadcom Wi-Fi case
md: Stateful targets need stateful fuzzing: keep a valid prefix, mutate later messages, use responses or coverage to recognise new states, and reset the target between sequences. Firmware that skips basic mitigations (no stack cookies) makes every such bug worse.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Filling the Wagner-Fischer table cell by cell
md: The table gives one number, but several different edit sequences can tie for the minimum. The traceback picks one of them. Do not read a single alignment as *the* explanation of how two strings differ.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
md: Invariant does not mean mirror-proof. Some cameras and optical paths flip the image. Astrometry.net's code-flip helper swaps each (x, y) pair, and the solver defaults to trying both parities (parity here means whether the image is mirrored or not). Groth's triangle method instead records whether vertices run clockwise and accepts either sense.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Radius search: cover with cells, then check exact distance
md: `WHERE ST_Distance(a, b) < 500` gives the right answer but cannot use the spatial index, so it scans every row. The PostGIS docs pair them deliberately: use `ST_DWithin` to limit the search with the index, then `ST_Distance` only for sorting the few survivors.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
md: Misconception: "nvidia-smi shows 20 GB used, so my tensors use 20 GB." It shows reserved memory plus the CUDA context: the driver's per-process state on the GPU, such as loaded kernel code and the driver's own buffers, which uses device memory that PyTorch's counters never include. Compare `memory_allocated()` with `memory_reserved()` before hunting for a leak.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: From registers to HBM: the GPU memory map
md: **Local memory is not local to the chip.** The word refers to scope (one thread), not location. Spilled registers, large per-thread arrays and arrays indexed with values the compiler cannot resolve at compile time all go to local memory, which has the latency and bandwidth of global memory.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Case study: one matrix transpose, three kernels
md: The NVIDIA post's conclusion: coalescing global memory accesses is by far the most critical step. Use shared memory to turn strided global access into coalesced access, then check the shared access for bank conflicts.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: How profiling perturbs what it measures
md: Decide which question you are asking before you choose the flags. Isolated-kernel analysis wants the defaults: locked clocks, flushed caches, serialized launches. System-representative behavior wants `--replay-mode application --clock-control none --cache-control none`. Mixing the two across runs produces numbers that disagree for reasons that have nothing to do with your code.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: From chunks to an entity graph with LLM extraction
md: The graph is an LLM's *abstractive summary* of the corpus (written in the model's own words, not copied sentences), not a parse of it. Every node and edge carries an LLM-written description, and those descriptions, not the raw text, are what later stages summarize.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: RLVR: replacing the reward model with a program
md: Verifiable does not mean perfect. A verifier can reject correct answers (12.0 versus 12) or accept wrong ones (a unit-test suite that misses edge cases). Real pipelines normalize answers; for example, Tulu 3's 'flex' MATH evaluation tries three different ways to extract the final answer, because models often ignore the requested format. The quality of the checker caps the quality of the signal.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: What a GTFS Schedule zip contains and how its tables join
md: A stop can appear twice in one trip, for example on a loop route where the bus starts and ends at the same stop. That is why `stop_sequence`, not `stop_id`, identifies a row of a trip. Code that keys stop times by `stop_id` alone silently overwrites one visit with the other.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf record: sampling on overflow, and the skid problem
md: Without precise sampling, the "hot" instruction in `perf annotate` is often the one *after* the slow one, such as the instruction that consumes a load's result. Use `:pp` when you care about individual instructions.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Hardware supply chain, coordinated disclosure, and practice
md: Hardware security in one sentence: the hardware runs your program correctly, but not invisibly. Keep secrets out of shared state (constant-time code, isolation, separate secure processors), keep firmware and microcode current, measure what booted, and expect new variants.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: CL.0 and client-side desync: when a server ignores the body
md: Every code path must leave the connection in a known state: either it consumed exactly the declared body, or it closes the connection. Cache hits, redirects, errors and static files are the paths that forget.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: What 4 KiB pages cost a 16 GiB working set
md: Huge pages pay off three ways: one TLB entry covers 512 (or 262,144) times more memory, each miss walks fewer levels, and the page tables shrink. The kernel's THP doc calls the fourth effect, one page fault per 2 MiB instead of 512, almost irrelevant because it only happens on first touch.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not
md: Pure SSMs are not simply worse. In the same NVIDIA study, Mamba-2 trained on 3.5T tokens beat the matching Transformer on average across standard zero-shot tasks. The gap is specific: copying, in-context learning and exact retrieval from the prompt.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion: fusing by rank, not score
md: RRF is not parameter-free. Bruch, Gai and Ingber (TOIS 2023, ACM Transactions on Information Systems) gave each retriever its own k and showed that nDCG swings noticeably when those constants are changed, and that constants tuned in-domain did not transfer reliably out of domain. Also, the window size is a hidden parameter: a document at rank 11 with a window of 10 contributes nothing at all.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How a PLC thinks: the scan cycle and ladder logic
md: Changing a setpoint and changing the program are different. Setpoints are data the program reads (often over the network, by design, from the HMI). The program is the logic itself. Both can steer the process; defenders must watch and protect both.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Ukraine 2015 and Industroyer 2016
md: It is tempting to read 2015 as 'malware turned off the lights'. Investigators found BlackEnergy but could not show it played a role in the outage; people turned off the lights, through legitimate remote access. Monitoring that only looks for malware would have missed it.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: One login, many apps: identity providers, service providers and trust
md: Misconception: SSO means one session. It means one *login*. After it, the IdP has a session and every app has its own, with its own cookie and lifetime. Disabling a user at the IdP does not end the app sessions already issued (lesson 10).

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Sessions across apps: IdP session, app sessions and logout
md: Offboarding gap: disabling a user at the IdP stops new logins, not existing app sessions or refresh tokens. A complete offboarding or account-takeover response also ends sessions in each app: through back-channel logout or signals where supported, through the app's admin API or SCIM deactivation (next lesson) where not.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Who has access, why, and who said so: identity governance
md: A common misconception is that identity and access management means single sign-on. Single sign-on proves who is logging in, once. It says nothing about whether Ana should still hold payroll access three jobs later. Governance works on the access itself, over time.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Just-in-time admin and break-glass accounts
md: A break-glass account that nobody monitors is just a permanent, policy-exempt Global Administrator. Its safety comes entirely from being rare, strongly authenticated, loudly alerted and regularly tested.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Cleaning the mask and correcting for lighting
md: Opening deletes every structure that cannot contain the kernel. A real change that is 1 or 2 pixels wide (a crack, a wire, a thin new road at low resolution) is erased along with the noise. Size the kernel from the smallest change you need to keep.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Evidence first: the order of volatility (RFC 3227)
md: RFC 3227 names programs to avoid on a live suspect system, such as `tar` or `xcopy`, because they update the access time of every file they touch, overwriting evidence of what the attacker read.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Communication: staff, customers, regulators and the legal clocks
md: Clocks start at awareness or determination, not at the end of the investigation. If you wait until you know everything, you will be late. Plan for phased notices: first what you know, then updates.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: MOVEit 2023: one SQL injection, thousands of victims
md: Patching closes the door but does not evict anyone already inside. After an injection that may have been exploited, look for persistence (web shells, new accounts, changed configuration) and for what data left, using web, database and network logs.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
md: io_uring turns I/O into **messages in shared memory**: batch them to amortize system calls, register files and buffers to cut per-request work, and use polling modes only where a spare CPU is worth the latency. The price is that correctness (lifetimes, ordering, CQ space) moves into your code.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Signed updates and anti-rollback: what a device must check
md: Fuses are a scarce, permanent budget. Bump the rollback version only when an old image has a security bug worth blocking, as MCUboot's separate security counter allows. Burn the bit only after the new image has proved it works (lesson 10), or a bad update could leave the device unable to boot anything.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Gadgets: from a polluted prototype to code execution (Kibana)
md: Do not read the hardening as "pollution is solved". It closes gadgets inside Node.js's own child_process code only. Your framework, template engine, HTTP client and your own options objects are full of optional properties, and every one is a possible gadget. The fix is still to stop pollution at the source.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Electron: when XSS in a desktop app becomes code execution
md: In Electron, every XSS is a candidate for code execution on the user's machine. The defaults (nodeIntegration off, contextIsolation on, sandbox on) are what keep XSS confined to the page; an app that turns any of them off, or runs an old Electron, has removed a wall. Lesson 16 covers the remaining walls you build yourself.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Histories: invoke, ok, fail, and the indeterminate info
md: Misconception: "a timeout means the request failed." A timeout means *you stopped waiting*. Writes, compare-and-sets and transaction commits that time out must be recorded as `:info` unless the error proves nothing was applied (for example, the request was rejected before it was sent).

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Measuring, caching and promoting without regressions
md: The most common autotuning self-deception is a "win" smaller than the confidence interval of the comparison. Report the interval, not just the ratio, and treat an interval that straddles 1.0 as "no difference found", not as a win.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The price of bypass, and when to choose something else
md: Bypass trades generality for cycles. It wins when per-operation overhead is the bottleneck and you can dedicate cores and devices; it loses when you need the kernel's protocols, tools, filesystems, isolation or power savings.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Temperature: amplifying the small probabilities
md: Temperature does not change the argmax, the class with the highest score. Running the deployed student at T greater than 1 does not change its top-1 predictions at all; it only makes its probabilities less confident. Temperature is a training-time device for distillation (and a separate sampling knob for generative models).

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: An LLM distillation pipeline: logits, tokenizers, traces, compute
md: Before writing an LLM distillation loss: confirm a teacher exists or will be reused; use logits when you can, text (Seq-KD, traces) when you cannot; store top-k with a tail bucket or mix in data loss; switch to a sorted-probability loss across tokenizers; and consider starting the student from a pruned teacher.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Quantizing keys per channel and values per token (KIVI)
md: Bits per number are not the whole cost. Group metadata adds bits (about 1 per number for FP16 scale and zero per 32), and the full-precision residual matters for short sequences.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Why the GPU prefix cache runs out, and where KV can go
md: Each tier down is roughly 10x bigger and slower. Offloading turns a prefix-cache miss into a load from a lower tier, which pays off only if the load is faster than recomputing.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Why wall clocks cannot order events across machines
md: A smaller wall-clock reading does not mean an event happened before another, and an event that did happen first can carry a larger wall-clock reading, as the last-write-wins example shows. Treat wall time as a hint, never as proof of order.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Storage: why token vectors are heavy and how ColBERTv2 shrinks them
md: Compression is lossy per vector, and the 1-bit setting does cost measurable quality. Treat 2-bit as the safe default and verify 1-bit on your own evaluation set before shipping it.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Teaching a model to think without words: the curriculum
md: The objective never asks a thought to compress the step it replaced. Thoughts are trained only by how much they help predict the remaining steps and the answer, so they are free to become something other than a paraphrase of the text.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: After Coconut: self-distillation, soft thinking, compressed latents
md: Later latent methods differ in what fills the next input slot: a distilled hidden state (CODI), a mixture of token embeddings (Soft Thinking), a sampled compressed embedding (CoLaR) or a discrete code (Token Assorted). Each fixes one of Coconut's limits, and none restores a fully readable trace.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Inserts, disks and when a learned index pays off
md: Bigtable's lesson: if you control the layout, make the data follow the model instead of making the model follow the data. Then the prediction is never wrong and there is no last-mile search across blocks.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaRank: weight each pair by what a swap does to NDCG
md: A lambda is a RankNet pair gradient scaled by how much the metric would change if the pair swapped. Pairs that cannot change the top of the list get almost no weight.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Gated DeltaNet: targeted writes plus fast forgetting
md: Gated DeltaNet's one-line change: decay first with a data-dependent $\alpha_t$, then do a delta-rule write with $\beta_t$. $\alpha_t\to0$ clears memory at a context switch; $\alpha_t\to1$ keeps it and lets the delta rule edit single associations.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Permission bits: rwx, octal, umask and the kernel's check
md: Owner, then group, then others: the first class that matches is the only one checked. Write octal as 4 for read, 2 for write, 1 for execute, and remember that umask removes bits from every new file.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Reading Linux logs: journald, auth.log, failed logins and sudo
md: The journal is stored on disk only if `/var/log/journal` exists or journald is configured with `Storage=persistent`. Otherwise it lives in memory under `/run/log/journal` and is lost at reboot (`journald.conf(5)`). Check this before you need the logs, not after an incident.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Tailoring, exceptions and rolling a baseline out safely
md: Tailor per host class, waive per host with an owner and an end date, and store both as code so an expired waiver fails on its own. Roll changes out in rings with a scan between rings.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: eBPF: small verified programs that watch the kernel from inside
md: eBPF lets a verified program run at a kernel hook and filter events in the kernel. That makes it the basis of modern Linux sensors. The verifier checks safety, not intent, so treat every BPF program load as a security event.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Case: Kinsing and TeamTNT, cryptominers on exposed Linux hosts
md: Cryptojacking chains are short and noisy: an exposed service, a root exploit, a service file, a hiding trick, a miner. A hardened, patched baseline breaks the first two steps, and the audit and eBPF rules from this course flag the rest.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Measuring judge agreement: confusion matrix and Cohen's kappa
md: Always say which agreement number you report. UMBRELA's GPT-4o labels on TREC DL 2019 to 2023 had 4-grade kappa 0.31 to 0.37 but binarised kappa 0.42 to 0.50 on the same labels. A paper quoting one and a dashboard quoting the other are not comparable.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Designing human evaluations and measuring agreement
md: Do not report raw percent agreement alone. With skewed labels (say 90% of pairs are ties) two annotators agree often by chance. Report kappa with the confusion matrix, and say how ties were handled.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: KV cache accounting: from bytes per token to batch size
md: Model weights are paid once; KV is paid per token per sequence. A common mistake is to size a deployment by "the model fits on the GPU". A model that fits with 2 GB to spare can serve almost nobody: 2 GB is only about 15,000 tokens of Llama 3 8B's KV cache.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Few-shot examples and asking the model to reason first
md: Examples fix the *format*; reasoning before the answer improves the *content* on multi-step problems. Both work only through the context the model reads before it commits to a token.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Ambiguity, negation and graceful fallback
md: Never silently drop a filter the user asked for. A validator that deletes an unknown value and runs the rest turns *rust engineers in Gotham* into *rust engineers anywhere*, and the user believes the results are in Gotham.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Cutting decode: FIRST and single-token listwise ranking
md: FIRST needs two things a plain chat API may not give you: logits over the identifier tokens at the first position, and a model whose first-token logits are trained or validated to rank well. With a zero-shot model, check that the logit order matches its generated order before trusting it.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Why sending every prompt to the strongest model wastes money
md: Routing pays off when two things are true at once: the price gap between models is large, and a sizable share of your prompts are ones where the weak model is just as good. If every prompt is hard, no router can save money without losing quality.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Matching descriptors and Lowe's ratio test
md: The ratio test needs at least two neighbors, so use `knnMatch(..., k=2)`. A matcher created with `crossCheck=True` is meant for `match()`, which returns one best match per descriptor.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Michael-Scott queue: a dummy node and helping
md: Helping is the general trick for multi-step lock-free updates: leave the structure in a state that any thread can recognise as half-finished and complete on the owner's behalf. Then no thread ever needs to wait for a specific other thread.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: From templates to counts, time series and alerts
md: T3's baseline is all zeros, so its MAD is 0 and the modified z-score divides by zero. Never let a never-fired template be scored this way: handle it with a separate **first-seen** rule that alerts the first time a template id appears, or when a template's lifetime count crosses a small bound. A miner that reports a new template id gives you that signal for free.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: The detection lifecycle: hypothesis to retirement
md: An alert without a written response is a notification nobody owns. If you cannot say what the analyst should do in the first ten minutes, the detection is not finished.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Why models break past their trained length
md: Each RoPE pair has a wavelength $\lambda_d = 2\pi b^{2d/|D|}$. Pairs with $\lambda_d \ll L$ are safe at any length; pairs with $\lambda_d > L$ are the ones that break when you go past the trained window.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Does the model use its context? Evaluation
md: Do not trust a single number. Low perplexity, a passing passkey test and a large advertised window can all coexist with poor use of mid-context information. Test retrieval at many depths, multi-hop and aggregation tasks, and short-context regressions.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Training for any loop count: random depth and truncated backprop
md: Random iteration counts teach one set of weights to work at many depths. Truncated backprop through only the last $k$ iterations keeps training memory independent of $r$, while the input injection still sends gradient to the prelude.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update
md: LoRA does not compress or approximate the pretrained weight. W0 keeps all its information at full rank. Only the *change* learned during fine-tuning is restricted to rank r.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Approximate unlearning: gradient ascent, collapse and NPO
md: "Loss on the forget set went up" (or its perplexity, $e$ to the average per-token loss, as in the prerequisite course) is not evidence of good unlearning. GA can drive that loss arbitrarily high by wrecking the model. Always read forget metrics next to utility metrics and next to the retrained reference.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Lab: unlearn TOFU authors with NPO, measure it, then quantize it
md: Our run is one seed of a 124M model on 20 authors, with a simplified utility and our own simulated quantizer. Use it to learn the workflow and the failure modes, not as evidence about which method is better at scale; for that, run the framework and report its full metrics.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Persistence on macOS: launchd, login items and BTM
md: Look beyond launchd: Microsoft's Shrootless research showed `~/.zshenv` runs for every zsh, including under `sudo`. Shell startup files, login items and browser extensions are all persistence. A new agent is cheap for the attacker; your job is to make it loud.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: What malware is, and the families analysts name
md: Do not trust the malware's own story. A ransom note, a file name or an icon is chosen by the author. Classify by what the code actually does: NotPetya's note said ransomware, its code said wiper.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Dynamic analysis: sandboxes, monitors and the WannaCry kill switch
md: Never register or contact infrastructure from a live sample without authorisation and coordination. Hutchins' registration worked out, but researchers who touch attacker infrastructure can disrupt investigations or alert attackers. In your lab, the internet is fake by design.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Why vector size is a cost knob, and why chopping a vector fails
md: Matryoshka training puts the most useful information in the first coordinates, so a prefix of the vector is a good small embedding. Without it, keeping the first m numbers of a normal embedding throws away information almost at random.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Pipeline parallelism: bubbles, 1F1B and the interleaved schedule
md: Bubble = (p - 1) / (v m). 1F1B bounds activation memory to p microbatches; interleaving divides the bubble by v at the cost of v times more pipeline sends.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Measuring the result: MFU, HFU and what the numbers count
md: Do not compare a paper's achieved TFLOP/s across systems without checking what it counts. Narayanan et al.'s 52% includes recomputation FLOPs; PaLM introduced MFU precisely because HFU depends on implementation choices like rematerialization (another name for recomputation).

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Know normal: the process tree, command lines and the PEB
md: Kernel-side data (EPROCESS, and the VADs of the next lesson) is what the process cannot easily edit; user-side data (PEB, loader lists, command line) is what it can. When they disagree, believe the kernel side and ask why the user side was changed.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Free memory you cannot use: two kinds of fragmentation
md: Fragmentation is not a leak. In a leak, *live* data grows because the program forgets to free. With fragmentation, live data is flat while the *footprint* grows. Tell them apart by comparing the bytes the allocator says are allocated with the memory it holds: a leak raises both, fragmentation widens the gap.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Relaxed: one agreed history per variable, nothing more
md: Myth: "Relaxed writes may take ages to show up, and SeqCst makes them visible sooner." The memory model says nothing about timing at all, only about order. A stronger ordering does not make data travel faster; it may even slow your program down.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Epoch-based reclamation: free garbage two epochs later
md: Holding a guard is holding back everyone's garbage. Pinning across a blocking call, a lock wait or a long iteration stops the epoch from advancing for all threads. crossbeam provides `Guard::repin` to briefly unpin and pin again inside long loops; references loaded before the repin are no longer protected.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Where things live: code, static data, heap and stack
md: The bug class tells you how memory is misused; the region tells you what gets damaged. Stack overflows threaten return addresses, heap overflows threaten neighbouring objects and allocator data.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Why re-ID needs an embedding space, not a classifier
md: A subtle limit of contrastive loss: it pulls every same-identity pair toward distance 0, so it tries to squash all images of one person onto a single point. The authors of FaceNet (Google's 2015 face recognition system, next lesson) argued that a triplet loss is better suited, because it only asks same-identity images to be closer than other identities, letting one person's images spread out along a region.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: When the optimizer deletes the code you meant to time
md: Misconception: "returning or summing the result is enough". Using the output defeats dead-code elimination, but not constant folding. The input must also come from somewhere the compiler cannot see through. JMH's constant-folding sample says to read inputs from non-final fields of a state object, and warns against making them `final` even when your IDE suggests it.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Miles in one picture: slime's loop built for frontier scale
md: The Miles docs do not publish a line-by-line diff against slime. This course teaches what Miles documents and measures; do not conclude from it that slime lacks any particular feature.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned policies leave a gap: LRU versus Belady's MIN
md: MIN is not a policy you can deploy, and it is not what learned caches try to predict exactly. It is a **yardstick**. Its value is telling you how big the gap is. On six production CDN traces with a 1 TB cache, the LRB authors measured a 25 to 40% gap in byte miss ratio (the fraction of requested bytes the cache could not serve) between MIN and the best online policies they tested.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Inside an APK and an IPA: what anyone can download and read
md: Legal note from the MASTG: in the US the DMCA (Digital Millennium Copyright Act, 17 U.S.C. 1201) makes circumventing some DRM illegal, with exemptions for certain security research. On a client engagement, ask the developer for unencrypted builds; it is faster and removes the question.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: The app is not the boundary: backend APIs seen through the app
md: A setting enforced only in the app's user interface is a display preference, not a privacy control. Test every privacy and permission setting by reading the raw API response.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Build an MLA layer and prove the two forms agree
md: Absorption is exact algebra, so a correct absorbed decoder matches the plain form to floating-point noise. Any larger gap is a bug, and the usual suspects are the norm, the RoPE split and the scale.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Thousands of adapters: S-LoRA's unified paging and loading
md: Unified Paging is not magic capacity. Adapter pages and KV pages come from the same pool, so many large adapters active at once shrink the space for KV cache and therefore the batch size. That is why clustering and rank choices still matter.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Why one scorer cannot be both cheap and accurate
md: Each stage has a different job. The first stage must not lose relevant documents (recall); precision barely matters there, because later stages discard junk. The last stage must put the best documents on top (precision at the top) and only has to be good on a short list.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Why lookahead helps, and where it does not
md: MTP reweights training toward decisions that matter for the continuation. It helps most on generative tasks such as code, at larger model sizes, with n tuned to the data; it is not a free win on every benchmark.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
